summary: Describes a way to keep network topology private when paths are computed across several domains by cooperating PCEs. Hidden segments of a path are replaced by an encrypted path key, so operators need not reveal their internal layout.

eli5.summary: A delivery company may not want to show competitors its secret routes. This note replaces the secret part of a route with a locked token that only that company can open.

questions: what is a path key in pce
how to keep topology confidential in inter-domain path computation
what is a confidential path segment
how does a pce hide topology between domains
subtitle: How a PCE can hand back a locked token instead of its internal path, so cooperating networks keep their topology private.

tldr.problem: When several Path Computation Elements (PCEs) cooperate to compute a path across domains, returning the path segment inside another provider's network would reveal that network's internal topology.
tldr.mechanism: The PCE replaces the Confidential Path Segment with a Path-Key Subobject, a small token holding a path-key and the ID of the PCE that can decode it. The router that must continue signaling later sends that token back to the PCE to get the real hops.
tldr.outcome: Confidentiality is kept while the full path is still computed in one go, which avoids the path diversity problem of loose hops. Both ends must support the new subobjects.

today: RFC 5520 is a Proposed Standard from April 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Confidentiality Problem
sections.content:
MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) can be computed by Path Computation Elements (PCEs). When an LSP crosses several domains, such as Autonomous Systems run by different service providers, each PCE computes the segment of the path in its own domain and the PCEs cooperate.

If the PCE in one domain simply returned its segment, the receiving PCE and the requesting client (the PCC) would see every hop through that domain. That breaks the confidentiality requirement of RFC 4105 and RFC 4216. The RFC calls the part that must stay hidden the Confidential Path Segment (CPS).

One workaround is to return a loose hop and let a border router run a fresh computation when signaling enters the next domain. That works for one LSP, but for several LSPs that should be disjoint (for protection, see RFC 5298) each expansion happens independently and unsynchronized, so disjointness cannot be guaranteed. With loose hops alone, confidentiality and path diversity are incompatible.
sections.eli5: A company will not show rivals its private roads. If it only says 'somewhere past our gate', each truck figures out its own way and two trucks may end up on the same road, even if you wanted them apart.

sections.title: The Path-Key Idea
sections.content:
A path-key is a token that replaces a path segment in an explicit route. It is an identifier allocated by a PCE, and the RFC stresses it has nothing to do with a cryptographic key.

The PCE puts the token in a Path-Key Subobject (PKS), which carries the path-key and the PCE's own identifier (the PCE ID). The entry boundary router of the CPS SHOULD appear, using its TE Router Id, as a hop just before the PKS. The PKS then travels in the explicit route object (ERO) of the RSVP-TE Path message like any other subobject, until it reaches the router that can expand it.

A path-key value is scoped to the PCE that issued it. The PCE ID in the PKS says which PCE can decode it.
sections.eli5: The ticket has a number and the name of the office that issued it. Only that office knows what the number means.

sections.title: How a Path-Key Is Issued and Expanded
sections.content:
When local policy says a segment must stay confidential, or the request asks for it, the PCE associates a path-key with the computed segment, builds a PKS and inserts it in the reply. The PCE SHOULD store the segment and key. Keeping it for 10 minutes is RECOMMENDED. A PCE MUST NOT reuse a path-key value for a new CPS for at least 30 minutes after discarding the old use. A PCE that cannot remember used values across a restart SHOULD embed something like a timestamp or version number.

The head-end router puts the path, including the PKS, in the ERO. When a router hits the PKS as its next hop, it takes the PCE ID from it and sends a PCReq message to that PCE with the PKS in a PATH-KEY object. The PCE looks up the stored segment and returns the real hops in an ERO inside the PCRep. The router splices them in and carries on setting up the LSP.

The RFC's example has two ASes. PCE-2 marks {ASBR-2, C, D, Egress} as the CPS and returns {ASBR-2, PKS, Egress}. PCE-1 gives the ingress {Ingress, A, B, ASBR-1, ASBR-2, PKS, Egress}. At ASBR-2 the PKS is expanded by asking PCE-2.
sections.eli5: Your truck carries the ticket through the first town. At the depot gate, the driver shows it to the office, gets the real directions and drives on.

sections.title: The Path-Key Subobject and PATH-KEY Object
sections.content:
The PKS is fixed length. It holds an L bit, a Type, a Length, a 16-bit Path-Key and a PCE ID. The L bit SHOULD NOT be set, so the subobject is a strict hop. Two forms exist so that IPv4 and IPv6 can both be used.

  • Type 64: PCE ID of 32 bits, Length always 8.
  • Type 65: PCE ID of 128 bits, Length always 20.

The PCE ID must be unique within the domain the CPS crosses and must be understood by the router that expands the PKS. It MAY be a reachable address of the PCE, but for more security or confidentiality it MAY be a value meaningful only inside the domain, such as a Router ID.

To ask for an expansion, the requester uses a new PATH-KEY object (Object-Class 16, Object-Type 1) and sets a new Path-Key bit in the RP object. The first PKS in the object MUST be processed, later ones SHOULD be ignored. In the PCReq message, a request is either a normal segment computation or a path-key-expansion containing just the PATH-KEY object.
sections.eli5: The ticket is a small card with a few boxes: a number and the name of the office. There is a short version and a longer version, depending on how long the office's name is.

sections.title: What Happens When Expansion Fails
sections.content:
An expansion request is an ordinary path computation request except that it MUST contain a PATH-KEY object and the Path-Key bit MUST be set. On a successful reply the requester SHOULD insert the CPS into the ERO it signals, according to local policy.

If the receiving PCE does not recognize its own ID in the PKS, it MAY forward the request to another PCE according to local policy, or else it MUST answer with a NO-PATH object. A PCE that recognizes itself but cannot find the CPS, or is not allowed by policy to release it, MUST also send NO-PATH. The NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV SHOULD be used with a new bit meaning 'Cannot expand PKS'.

On a negative reply the requesting router MUST fail the LSP setup and SHOULD use the procedures for loose hop expansion failure from RFC 3209.
sections.eli5: If the office cannot find your ticket, or is not allowed to give out the directions, it says so and the trip is called off.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The RFC describes tunneling confidential path information across an untrusted domain. It lists three concerns: whether others can probe for expansions, whether a path-key can be altered or faked, and denial-of-service through spurious keys or floods of bogus requests. Most interactions are point to point and can be secured with the mechanisms of RFC 5440 and RFC 3209. A rogue router could modify the ERO, but that is described as an existing RSVP problem not addressed here.

A PCE answering a decode request is recommended to check that the asking router is the head end of the decoded segment. Using a PCE ID that only means something inside the domain gives further protection.

On manageability, replacing segments with a PKS MUST be under operator and policy control. The retention and reuse timers SHOULD be configurable. A new MIB module MUST be created to inspect path-keys, and a PCE SHOULD keep counters and logs for attempts to expand unknown or expired keys, duplicate attempts, and keys that expire unused.
sections.eli5: Only the right depot should be able to swap a ticket for directions, so the office checks who is asking. Bosses also get to decide which routes are hidden.

sections.title: Deployment Effects and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
Only the head-end routers that build the RSVP-TE Path message and the routers that must expand a PKS need changes. Other routers on the path pass the PKS along untouched. A PCE will not supply a PKS unless it knows the receiving router can handle it. A legacy head end that gets a PKS it cannot encode must either fail the setup or ask for a new path that avoids that domain.

The RFC also notes a scaling benefit: one PKS can stand in for many subobjects, shrinking message size, which can matter for point-to-multipoint LSPs.

IANA assigned ERO subobject types 64 and 65, the PATH-KEY object (class 16, type 1), bit 23 in the RP object for the Path-Key flag, and bit 27 in the NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV for PKS expansion failure.
sections.eli5: Only the trucks and depots that use tickets need to learn about them. The rest of the roads work as before.
